lines.text: # Proposal: closing the Telegram-delivery criterion
## Status of the referenced handoff doc
The operator's request points at `research/telegram-bot-setup.md` as the
handoff doc with the exact code gap and diff. In this worktree, `research/`
does not exist at all (`ls research/` fails with "No such file or
directory"). This proposal cannot read, quote, or build on that file's
contents, and does not claim otherwise. Whatever this proposal says about the
code gap is stated from the operator's verbatim description only:
`notifications.py:_reach()` never passes `token`/`chat_id` to `reach.send()`.
This proposal does not write to `research/`, `gates/`, or
`pravrudhi_kernel/`, and does not touch the ledger. Everything below is a
plan, not a result.
## Why nothing in this sandbox can be evidence
This sandbox has no network access and no write access outside
`proposals/requests/r-0704b2a0/0/`. That means two things are both true here:
- No call to a real Telegram Bot API endpoint can be made, so no delivery to
chat id `<redacted:telegram-chat-id>` can happen from this proposal.
- No write to `notifications.record()`'s ledger, and no edit to
`pravrudhi_kernel/` or `gates/`, can happen from this proposal, so no code
fix and no recorded notification can originate here either.
Per the operator's own framing (echoing the prior rejection), the criterion
closes only when a human who can see **both** the ledger entry produced by
`notifications.record()` **and** the real Telegram chat observes the message
arrive. That observation cannot be produced, simulated, or asserted from a
sandboxed proposal step — including by printing a number, a percentage, or a
"delivered: true"-style flag, none of which this file or its scripts do.
## Approach (what should happen, outside this sandbox)
1. **Code fix**, applied to `pravrudhi_kernel/notifications.py` (not here —
this sandbox cannot write there): in `_reach()`, resolve Telegram
credentials via `messaging.resolve_telegram()` (which reads
`~/.config/pravrudhi/telegram.env`, the file the `EnvironmentFile` line in
the systemd units already points at) and pass the resulting `token` and
`chat_id` through to `reach.send(...)`, instead of calling `reach.send()`
with those arguments omitted.
2. **Offline check**, run outside this sandbox by a session with write access
to `pravrudhi_kernel/` and `research/`: a unit test that mocks
`reach.send` and asserts `_reach()` calls `messaging.resolve_telegram()`
and forwards its `token`/`chat_id` into the mocked call. This proves the
wiring is correct without touching the network. See
`check_reach_credential_wiring.py` in this directory for a runnable sketch
of that test — it is not executed as part of this proposal, and this
proposal does not run it or report a pass/fail from it.
3. **Live check**, run outside this sandbox, with network access, by whoever
restarts `pravrudhi-app.service` (or otherwise reloads the fixed code) on
the operator's host:
- Call `notifications.record(...)` (or trigger whatever real event calls
it) on the operator's engine root.
- Confirm two things exist, independently: a new ledger entry from that
call, and a new message in the `@pravrudhi_bot` conversation with chat
- Only a person (or an agent turn with tool access to both the ledger and
the Telegram chat) who directly observes both artifacts can close this
criterion. That observation is the deliverable this proposal cannot
produce.
## What would count as evidence
A statement, made by whoever can see both the ledger and the Telegram chat
after the code fix lands and the service is restarted, that:
- a specific `notifications.record()` call (identified by its ledger entry)
- corresponds to a specific message that arrived in the real
`@pravrudhi_bot` → chat `8679892510` conversation,
with both artifacts named concretely enough that a third party could go
verify them independently (e.g. a ledger entry id/timestamp and a
description of the Telegram message that arrived at the corresponding time).
No count, percentage, or "N messages delivered" style figure is a substitute
for that paired observation, and this proposal supplies none.
## Files in this proposal
- `README.md` — this file.
- `check_reach_credential_wiring.py` — a syntactically valid, not-executed
sketch of the offline unit test described in step 2 above. It imports
nothing that resolves inside this sandbox's write restrictions and is
provided only as a starting point for the session that has
`pravrudhi_kernel/` write access to adapt and actually run.
"""Sketch of the offline wiring check described in README.md, step 2.
This file is NOT executed as part of this proposal. It is not run here, it
writes nothing to any ledger, and it reports no result. It exists only so a
session with write access to `pravrudhi_kernel/` can adapt it into a real
test once `_reach()` is fixed to resolve and forward Telegram credentials.
Running this (elsewhere, with the fix applied) would prove only that
`_reach()` calls `messaging.resolve_telegram()` and forwards the resulting
token/chat_id into `reach.send()`. It proves the wiring is correct; it does
not and cannot prove that a real Telegram message was delivered, because it
mocks `reach.send` instead of calling it.
from __future__ import annotations
from unittest.mock import MagicMock, patch
def check_reach_forwards_resolved_credentials() -> None:
"""Sketch: `_reach()` must pass resolve_telegram()'s token/chat_id to reach.send()."""
from pravrudhi_kernel import messaging, notifications
fake_token = "PLACEHOLDER-token"
fake_chat_id = "PLACEHOLDER-chat-id"
with patch.object(
messaging, "resolve_telegram", return_value=(fake_token, fake_chat_id)
), patch.object(notifications, "reach") as fake_reach:
fake_reach.send = MagicMock()
notifications._reach("PLACEHOLDER-message")
fake_reach.send.assert_called_once()
_, called_kwargs = fake_reach.send.call_args
assert called_kwargs.get("token") == fake_token
assert called_kwargs.get("chat_id") == fake_chat_id
if __name__ == "__main__":
raise SystemExit(
"This script is a proposal sketch and is intentionally not runnable "
"here: it depends on pravrudhi_kernel internals this sandbox cannot "
"write to or execute against, and it must never be reported as a "
"result from within proposals/. Run it only from a session with "
"pravrudhi_kernel/ write access, after the _reach() fix lands."
# Proposal: evidence that `alibaba-plan` resolves its key from `dashscope-plan.env` and reaches the plan-exclusive endpoint
## What this round is, and is not
This is a proposal, not evidence. It lives under `proposals/`, has never been executed by the
project's real test runner, and no outcome from it is recorded in the ledger. Per the operating
charter for this round: no number, percentage, or score written here may be read as a result, even
one labeled fabricated, simulated, hypothetical, illustrative, or a placeholder — so the draft test
below uses non-numeric stand-ins (`PLACEHOLDER-FREE-TIER-KEY`, `PLACEHOLDER-PLAN-KEY`, a literal
`"PLACEHOLDER"` prompt) everywhere a script needs a value to run. The oldest unmet acceptance
criterion is satisfied only once a test like this one exists under `tests/`, is run by `uv run
pytest` (or whatever the project's real runner is), and that run's outcome is written to the
ledger — none of which this round is permitted to do (sandbox network access is `none`, and
`pravrudhi_kernel/`, `research/`, `gates/`, and the ledger are all off-limits from here).
## Context this proposal corrects against the prior round
The prior round's feedback, restated for this round so it isn't lost again:
- The provider under test is `alibaba-plan`, Alibaba's **Lite Plan** tier — not the free tier. The
two are deliberately modeled as separate providers in
`src/pravrudhi/agents/alibaba_agent.py` (`CREDENTIAL_NAMES = {"alibaba": "dashscope.env",
"alibaba-plan": "dashscope-plan.env"}`) precisely because a Lite Plan key sent to the free-tier
endpoint, or vice versa, fails in a way that reads like a bad key rather than a wrong endpoint.
- Both credential files use the same variable name, `DASHSCOPE_API_KEY` (`KEY_NAME` in that
module) — the two tiers are told apart by **which file** the key was read from
(`~/.config/llm/dashscope-plan.env` vs `~/.config/llm/dashscope.env`), never by the variable
name. A test that only checks the variable name, without pinning down the file, would not prove
the criterion.
- `src/pravrudhi/application/credentials.py` gives the two tiers genuinely different `base_url`
values: `alibaba` points at `dashscope-intl.aliyuncs.com/compatible-mode/v1` (free tier),
`alibaba-plan` points at `token-plan.ap-southeast-1.maas.aliyuncs.com/compatible-mode/v1`
(plan-exclusive). "Reaches the plan-exclusive endpoint" means the outbound `baseURL` in
`alibaba_agent.configuration(model, "alibaba-plan")` must be the latter, not the former.
- The desktop app is bring-your-own-key for every model provider it supports: it does not ship,
route, or proxy any provider's API on a user's behalf, and a user must configure their own
credential in the desktop app before any provider there becomes usable. The `~/.config/llm/dashscope-plan.env`
path this criterion is about is **not** that per-user desktop mechanism — it is the credential
the core Pravrudhi service itself (its own agents, e.g. this repository's build/CI dispatch) uses
to reach Alibaba's Lite Plan. This test is about proving core Pravrudhi's own credential
resolution is correct and isolated from the free-tier file; it says nothing about, and does not
need to exercise, any desktop-side provider configuration.
- The operator has stated the real `dashscope-plan.env` key is already in place on their machine
and has been tested manually. That real key and any result from using it belongs in the ledger
once a real run happens under the real test runner — this proposal must not restate, imply, or
fabricate a number standing in for that outcome.
## Approach
Prove the criterion with a unit-level test that never touches the network or the operator's real
credential files, plus a description of the one additional integration check that would need the
operator's real key and is explicitly out of scope for this sandboxed round.
### Unit-level test (draft: `draft_test_alibaba_plan.py`, sketch only — becomes evidence once an
equivalent lands in `tests/` and is run for real)
The draft exercises `pravrudhi.agents.alibaba_agent` directly:
1. **File isolation, not variable-name isolation.** Monkeypatch `Path.home()` to a `tmp_path`,
write two fake credential files under `<tmp_path>/.config/llm/`: `dashscope.env` carrying a
free-tier placeholder value and `dashscope-plan.env` carrying a plan placeholder value — both
using the same `DASHSCOPE_API_KEY` line, mirroring production. Call
`alibaba_agent.credential("alibaba-plan")` and assert the returned secret equals the plan
placeholder and never the free-tier one. This is the direct test that a free-tier key is never
sent to the plan path.
2. **Path resolution.** Assert `alibaba_agent.credential_path("alibaba-plan")` resolves to
`<home>/.config/llm/dashscope-plan.env` specifically (not just "some file"), and that
`credential_path("alibaba")` resolves to the sibling `dashscope.env`, so the two are proven
distinct rather than coincidentally equal.

# IDE surface: pick Claude Code / Codex / OpenRouter per task
Status: design note only. Nothing here is implemented, and nothing here is a
result — every route id, provider id and field name below names something
that already exists in the checked-in source, cited by path, not a measured
outcome.
## What already exists (read, not guessed)
- **`configs/routing.yaml`** is the routing table the operator's request
called "routes.yaml". Each entry is a *route*: an `agent` (`claude-code`,
`codex`, `hosted`, `loop`, `orca:local`, ...), a `model`, the `tiers` it is
eligible for, and a `relative_cost` used to break ties. This is the table a
per-task picker would ultimately be choosing *from* — it is the source of
truth for "which agents exist and what tiers they may run at," not
something a UI should duplicate.
- **`/api/providers`** (`src/pravrudhi/api/server.py`, the `providers_ep`
handler) is the bring-your-own-key registry: for the calling user's
project, it reports each provider (`openai`, `anthropic`, `google`,
`alibaba`, `alibaba-plan`, `openai-compatible`, defined in
`src/pravrudhi/application/credentials.py`) as configured or not, never the
key itself. `POST /api/providers/{id}/key` and `DELETE
/api/providers/{id}/key` are how a key is set or removed. There is no
`openrouter` entry yet, but `openai-compatible` already models "an
OpenAI-shaped API with a base URL and a bearer key," which is exactly what
OpenRouter is — adding an `openrouter` provider (or a preset base URL on
`openai-compatible`) is a registry entry, not a new mechanism.
- **The swarm page** (`app/frontend/src/app/swarm/page.tsx`) already renders
a Dispatch section (`app/frontend/src/components/swarm/DispatchPanel.tsx`)
that lets an operator hand the swarm an ad hoc brief: title, brief, allowed
paths, validate command, tier, sandbox policy, and — already present today
— a free-text **"Pin an agent (optional)"** field. That field's value flows
straight through `JobInput.agent` (`app/frontend/src/lib/swarm.ts`) to
`POST /api/jobs`. In other words: the per-task "which agent handles this"
control the operator is asking for already has a seam in the UI and the
API; it is currently an unvalidated free-text box instead of a picker
backed by what is actually usable.
- The same page's `LivePanel`/`FleetTable`/`RoutingTable` already fetch
`/api/swarm`, whose response (`SwarmSnapshot` in `app/frontend/src/lib/
swarm.ts`) includes a `roster` of `Seat` objects — each seat already
carries `agent`, `model`, `tiers`, and a `usable` flag. That is close to,
but not the same as, "is this seat available to *this signed-in user*,"
because usability today reflects the operator's own configured routes and
quotas, not a per-user BYOK key.
## The gap
Nothing today lets a user, from the interface, say "run *this* task with
Claude Code" vs "with Codex" vs "with an OpenRouter model I've supplied a key
for," where the choice is constrained to options that will actually work for
*them* (their own configured provider keys) rather than a free-text field
that can name a route id that does not exist or is not usable by that
caller.
## Proposed approach
Extend, in this order, rather than build a parallel surface:
1. **No new backend route for the first slice.** The swarm page already
fetches both `/api/swarm` (for `roster`) and could fetch `/api/providers`
in the same load. Replace the DispatchPanel's free-text "Pin an agent"
input with a `<select>` populated from `roster`, each option showing
`agent` / `model` / `tier` eligibility, and disabled when the route's
underlying provider (matched by the route's `agent` field, e.g.
`claude-code` → `anthropic`, `codex` → `openai`, a prospective
`openrouter` route → `openrouter`) is not `configured` per
`/api/providers`. This is a frontend-only change: no schema change, no new
endpoint, because both data sources already exist and are already
fetched on adjacent parts of the same page.
2. **Second slice — validate server-side.** Today `dispatchboard.py`
presumably accepts `agent` as an opaque optional string (the API layer
already treats it that way per `JobInput.agent: string | null`). Add
server-side validation in the job-creation handler that rejects an
`agent`/route id that is not both (a) present in `configs/routing.yaml`
and (b) backed by a configured provider key for the caller, with a 422
and a reason — the same shape `set_provider_key` already uses for
validation failures. This turns "silently falls back to the router's
choice" into "tells the user why their pin was refused."
3. **Third slice — a dedicated `GET /api/routes`.** Once the picker needs
more than the swarm snapshot already provides (e.g. per-route
descriptions, or routes that are configured but not currently in the
roster because they've never been dispatched), add a small read-only
endpoint that joins `configs/routing.yaml` against the caller's
`/api/providers` configured set, so the frontend stops having to
cross-reference two responses itself. This is additive and does not
require touching the first two slices.
4. **OpenRouter specifically** needs one registry entry (`openrouter` in
`PROVIDERS`, `src/pravrudhi/application/credentials.py`, following the
`openai-compatible` shape with OpenRouter's base URL and key prefix) plus
one or more routes in `configs/routing.yaml` naming it as the `agent`
(however that agent is invoked — that plumbing is outside this note).
Nothing about the picker UI changes to support it: it is just another row
once the registry and routing table know about it.
The point of ordering it this way is that slice 1 ships with zero backend
change and turns an already-broken affordance (free text that can name
nothing real) into a working one, and each later slice is additive rather
than a rewrite of the one before it.
## What would count as evidence this criterion is met
This criterion is about the design note existing and being accurate, not
about the feature shipping. Evidence would be:
- This README (or its successor) accurately naming the extension points —
`configs/routing.yaml`, `/api/providers`, the swarm page's DispatchPanel —
against whatever those files contain at review time, since they are
expected to keep moving.
- A reviewer being able to trace, from this note alone, exactly which
existing file each proposed slice touches and which fields it reads, with
no invented endpoint or field that is not either (a) cited above as
already existing or (b) explicitly marked as new in "Proposed approach."
- The smallest slice (item 1) being buildable without any change outside
`app/frontend/src/components/swarm/DispatchPanel.tsx` and, if the fetch is
added there, `app/frontend/src/lib/swarm.ts` — i.e. that the claim "no
backend change needed for the first slice" holds up when someone tries it.
- This directory containing no implementation of the picker itself — only
the sketch in `sketch_routes_view.py`, which documents shapes and is not
wired into the running application.
## Files here
- `README.md` — this note.
- `sketch_routes_view.py` — a non-executable sketch (dataclasses only, no
logic, no network, no imports from `pravrudhi_kernel`/`src`) of the shapes
a future `GET /api/routes` response and the picker's option list might
take, to make slice 3 concrete without writing the endpoint.

objectives.intent: A scaffolding harness that makes a fixed model write correct Python more often, changed only in how the model is prompted and how its output is checked, never in the model's weights.
objectives.notes: The internal pool selected a harness change that the external scorer then contradicted. That contradiction is in the ledger and this objective renders it rather than hiding it; a promotion the external tier refuses is the most useful row the loop has produced.

objectives.intent: A small model that solves grade-school arithmetic word problems more reliably than the checkpoint it started from, without losing what it already knew.
objectives.notes: Scored by lm-evaluation-harness outside the kernel, on the held-out test split, and admitted to the ledger by file hash. The internal sealed pool is the loop's selection instrument and is not this objective's evidence.

objectives.intent: An orchestration strategy that makes a fixed model solve more programming problems correctly, changed only in how work is decomposed, dispatched, checked and retried across one or more agents, never in the model's weights. The engine's own single-agent harness is the incumbent every candidate is paired against, so a strategy that adds coordination without adding correctness is visible as such rather than assumed better.
objectives.notes:
What a candidate is: a named strategy expressed in the harness grammar. A single agent with retries is the incumbent. A planner that decomposes then executes, a proposer-and-critic pair, a fan-out that solves the same problem several ways and selects, and a graph with explicit state between steps are all candidates, and each is what the frameworks on the market actually implement underneath their APIs.
Adopting a framework is therefore the second question, not the first. If decomposition beats a single agent on these benchmarks, the framework that expresses decomposition well is worth its dependency; if it does not, no framework's ergonomics will help, and this engine will have learned that for the price of a few nights rather than a rewrite.
The likeliest outcome, stated in advance so its arrival is informative rather than disappointing: coordination costs tokens and adds failure modes, and on problems a single agent already solves it will lose. The interesting result would be a strategy that wins specifically on the problems the incumbent fails, which is a question about where the gains are rather than whether the mean moved.

objectives.intent: A legal-reasoning assistant for Indian jurisprudence that answers a question of law with the statute or precedent it relied on, and that says it does not know rather than inventing a citation. The reasoning is to run over a typed Nyaya meaning graph rather than over surface text, so that a wrong answer can be traced to the inference step that produced it.
objectives.notes: Cited-statute accuracy is the metric this objective actually wants and no public harness scores it. The two MMLU law subtasks are stand-ins that move for the right reasons; treat them as a proxy and say so, rather than reporting them as if they measured citation faithfulness.

rows.notes: The server streams and the client now reads the body incrementally rather than awaiting the whole response. Still partial because the end-to-end test has not passed. This machine has no chat model configured, so /api/chat answers 503 and the test cannot observe any tokens at all. The test asserts the answer was seen growing at least twice, since a blocking response yields exactly one observation and would satisfy a weaker bar. It stays partial until it runs green against a configured model.
rows.why_it_matters: Receive progress while an answer is produced.

rows.notes: The in-app bell is mounted, and a notification is also delivered to Telegram - the operator's engine through its own environment, a user's workspace through a bot they add in settings, and never one through the other. OS notifications are still not claimed.
rows.why_it_matters: Notice completed work without polling a work panel.

rows.notes: Run rather than read, and now as two installs. Studio and the product are separate builds with their own appId, product name, output directory and per-user data directory, so both sit on one machine without overwriting each other, and each carries an edition file the app reads and passes to every engine it starts. Both were installed on Linux and on the Mac mini, and each reported launched, engine found, health ok, no errors, and the edition it was built as, against an engine it started itself. Unit tests cover port selection, process ownership, teardown, the edition rule and the two build configurations. Three caveats stay in view. Windows is built by release CI and has never been launched, so nothing here claims it runs; the Linux launch passes --no-sandbox because that machine's Electron sandbox helper needs root; and the macOS build is unsigned and not notarized, which is fine for the operator's own machines and not for distribution.
rows.why_it_matters: Keep the local engine in a dedicated application window.

rows.notes: Source-level System page; actual health depends on live data.
rows.why_it_matters: Understand the engine and available builders.

rows.notes: Both isolate agents per worktree. Ours also merges them three-way per file and names a contested file rather than letting the last writer win, which was added after five silent overwrites in one day.
rows.why_it_matters: Run several agents at once without them overwriting each other.

rows.notes: A run's output streams into the interface as it happens, over the same server-sent events the engine already publishes, with scrollback and follow-the-tail. Partial rather than have, and deliberately so: it accepts no typed input. A shell in a web page is a remote execution surface and this engine's threat model does not have one, so the gap against Orca here is a decision rather than unfinished work.
rows.why_it_matters: Run and watch a command without leaving the application.

rows.why_it_matters: Review and land work without switching to a browser.

rows.capability: Drag a file into the conversation
rows.notes:
A file dropped on the composer is read in the browser and its text folded into the message, since this engine has no upload route and none was added. The limits are therefore the whole of the protection and are stated as named constants with their reasons: 256 KB a file, 512 KB in total, four at once, text and source formats only. Every refusal carries its own sentence rather than failing silently.
The evidence names the page as well as the components, deliberately. They existed for a while mounted on nothing, exactly as the command palette once did, and this row stayed at none for as long as that was true.
rows.why_it_matters: Attach context without typing a path.

rows.notes: A note attaches to a file and line of a task's diff, several to a line, and the set for a task reads as a whole because the reason to write them is to hand them to someone. They live in the browser: an annotation is one reviewer's working note, the engine has no route to store one, and a blocked storage API degrades to notes that last the session rather than breaking the page.
rows.why_it_matters: Say what is wrong with a change at the line it is wrong on.

rows.why_it_matters: Work without reaching for the pointer.

rows.capability: Edit a document in the application
rows.notes: A note is written, corrected in place and deleted, with a Markdown source/preview editor over a renderer whose escaping and scheme allowlist are tested as attacks. The claim is the round trip rather than the widget - the editor existed for a while with its Save button wired to nothing, which is why the evidence is the API test and the page's handler rather than the component's presence.
rows.why_it_matters: Keep notes and plans where the work is.

rows.capability: Choose the agent and model from measured outcomes
rows.notes: A route is picked as the cheapest whose Wilson interval upper bound still reaches the best route's lower bound, so a cheap route is kept until the log can actually tell them apart. The claim is the rule and its recorded outcomes, not that the ranking is correct - on 2026-09-08 the Lite Plan seat stood at two successes in six trials, an interval of 0.10 to 0.70, which distinguishes it from nothing yet.
rows.why_it_matters: Spend on the expensive route only once the evidence distinguishes it from a cheaper one.

rows.capability: Every stated number traces to an append-only ledger row
rows.notes: The ledger is written once and verified as a chain, and replay folds it back into the state a night saw. The scope is the mechanism; it does not assert that every surface in the product reads from it.
rows.why_it_matters: A result that cannot be replayed from its own record is a claim, not a measurement.

rows.capability: Read back the parent structure of the search
rows.notes: The lineage field was written on every proposal from the start and read by nothing. Folded, the committed ledger gives 189 candidates, two distinct parents and a maximum depth of two - a two-node star, which is recorded here as the shape the search currently has rather than as an achievement.
rows.why_it_matters: Without ancestry an evolutionary arm has nothing to shrink toward and no novelty to reward.

rows.capability: Report whether the budget forced a choice at all
rows.notes: Per night, the live pool against what was run. On the committed ledger the budget bound on seven of sixteen nights, so on the other nine the controller ranked a set it was going to run in full. This row exists to keep that measurable; it is the least flattering number the engine reports about itself.
rows.why_it_matters: A selection rule earns nothing on a night when everything proposed could be afforded.

rows.capability: Run unattended within a declared appetite
rows.notes: A night proposes, measures and prunes without intervention, and the drives that choose what to do next are weighted by a checked-in appetite policy an operator can override per workspace. The claim is that it runs unattended and bounded, not that any given night improved anything.
rows.why_it_matters: Improvement that needs an operator present is not improvement the operator can leave running.

`LinkedActivity.tsx` renders three visually and textually distinct states — unknown (source unavailable), successfully-empty (source returned no activity), and populated — such that the unknown state neither displays a count nor reads as an absence of activity, and the successfully-empty state is only reachable from a successful fetch.

completion gate refused: ## Finding: criterion [0] fails — no agent actually persists on parity; the only autonomous loop explicitly excludes it

I read the cited evidence file (`completion.py`) and traced where "parity" actually lives in the codebase, since `completion.py` itself contains nothing about Orca, parity, or rivalry — it's a generic evidence-verification/adversarial-review gate applicable to any request.

The real parity machinery is `src/pravrudhi/application/parity.py` + `src/pravrudhi/assets/configs/parity.yaml`: a hand-edited YAML capability matrix with self-checking evidence (`grep`/test commands), exposed read-only through a CLI command (`pravrudhi parity`) and `/api/parity`. Nothing in that path is an agent that *persists* — it's a static table a human (or an ad hoc agent session) edits when prompted.

The one candidate for an actual persistent/autonomous agent is the heartbeat (`src/pravrudhi/application/heartbeat.py`, driven by `pravrudhi-heartbeat.timer`), which wakes on a schedule and dispatches work against the engine's six-then-seven "drives" in `kshudha.py`. Rivalry against named competitors is modeled there as `spardha_drive` (kshudha.py:394) — but it computes gaps only against *declared benchmark scores* (e.g. GSM8K), not UX/feature parity, and it is not wired into the heartbeat's dispatch table at all: `heartbeat.py`'s `_action_for` only handles `samarthya`, `seva`, `sthiti`, with `sadhana` falling back to a no-op desire log and `pramana_navyata`/`unnati_avakasha` explicitly producing "a bounded diagnostic, never a fabricated [action]." `spardha` doesn't appear in `_action_for` at all — grepping `heartbeat.py` for `spardha` returns nothing.

The codebase's own commentary in `parity.yaml` concedes this directly: it notes OpenClaw has "an autonomous loop that executes (autonomousLoop.js) where this engine's heartbeat only chooses" — i.e., the project's own record states that, unlike the rival being compared against, nothing here turns a parity gap into dispatched, executed work on its own. The OpenClaw row itself was filled in only after "the completion gate's adversarial reviewer correctly called out" that it had sat at `unknown` despite being named twice — meaning the parity table's accuracy depends on someone manually noticing the gap and then manually researching and hand-editing the YAML, not on a dedicated agent that persists on the work.

So criterion [0]'s evidence file does not establish what it claims. There is a parity *report* and a generic evidence-verification *gate*, but no agent — scheduled or otherwise — whose job is to keep working toward closing feature/UX gaps against Orca (or Claude Desktop, Codex, OpenClaw). This does not satisfy the operator's explicit ask to "dedicate an agent to persist on it."

## Secondary finding: criterion [3]'s "real clicks" demo is a static slideshow, not an interactive demonstration

completion gate refused: ## Finding: criterion [0]/[1] — "every operator ask" is not actually captured by Pravrudhi

The evidence for criterion [0] cites `src/pravrudhi/application/requests.py` as proof that "every operator ask is captured in a log inside Pravrudhi." Reading that module shows it is a well-built, passive data layer: a `Request`/`Criterion` dataclass model, a JSON store under `.pravrudhi/requests.json`, a state machine, and a `capture()` function — but `capture()` only runs when something calls it. The module itself has no listener on any input channel; it cannot capture anything on its own.

I traced what actually calls `capture()`/`requests-capture` in the shipped code:

- `src/pravrudhi/application/watchdog.py` and `src/pravrudhi/application/telegram_inbox.py` call it directly.
- `pravrudhi/cli/app.py` exposes it as `requests-capture`, a CLI command someone (or something) must invoke.
- Pravrudhi's own chat surface, `src/pravrudhi/application/chat.py` (the very file cited in criterion [5] as the engine's first-person voice), **never calls `capture` at all** — a `grep` for `capture` in that file returns nothing.

The actual mechanism that makes "every ask you type to me right now" land in the ledger is `.claude/hooks/capture-ask.py`, registered via `.claude/settings.json` as a `UserPromptSubmit` hook, which shells out to `pravrudhi requests-capture`. I confirmed with `git check-ignore -v` that **both `.claude/` (the hook and its registration) and `.pravrudhi/` (the ledger file itself) are gitignored** by this repository's own `.gitignore` (lines 14–15). None of this ships with Pravrudhi. A fresh clone, a different machine, a different agent in the swarm (Codex, Astra, the desktop app), or this same operator talking to Pravrudhi through any surface other than this specific Claude Code session on this specific machine, has no automatic capture at all.

Even where the hook is installed, it does not capture "every" ask by its own documented design (confirmed against the operator's own prior memory note on this exact mechanism): it skips prompts under 80 characters, skips prompts containing harness markers, skips near-duplicates, and **swallows every failure silently** — so if the hook script breaks, asks stop being recorded with no signal from inside Pravrudhi that anything was missed. The memory record documents this already happened once: five substantial asks went uncaptured in one afternoon.

So the acceptance criterion's evidence is real and the cited code is solid, but it demonstrates a manual/optional ledger API plus two narrow integrations (Telegram, a watchdog) — not the property actually asked for, which was that the *engine itself* durably remembers every ask made of it. The thing that makes that true today is external, per-machine, best-effort, and explicitly excluded from the product by its own `.gitignore`. That is a materially different, and much weaker, guarantee than "every operator ask goes into a log inside Pravrudhi," and it is the exact failure mode (an ask silently going unlogged) the operator's original request was trying to rule out.

I did not exhaustively re-verify every other numbered criterion (0–12) to the same depth given the scope of this review, but this one is sufficient on its own: it undermines the foundational claim the operator's request opened with, and the same gap likely also weakens criterion [2] (the heartbeat "works the oldest unmet ask on its own" — it can only work asks that made it into the ledger in the first place).

Treat that as the standing rule.

Not commits, not analysis, not internal metrics. Autonomous value, externally provable. They also said "don't compromise the speed, breadth and depth of the work just to save tokens" — economise on waste, never on depth.

*Accounts.* `~/.claude` is now a second premium seat on the same Axis Meru team plan (sharath.sathish@gmail.com, default_claude_max_5x). NOT a CHARTER breach: the rule targets the operator's personal PLAN exhausting mid-run (it cost gate A1.1 12 of 80 prompts), not the mailbox domain. <cross-session-message from="local_3d82679c-ad49-4ba3-a4bc-f95dbdee1a98" name="Studio and product autonomy assessment">
Operator relay — adversarial review of the Studio/Product desktop apps and connected web apps, run just now via an 18-agent workflow (6 dimension audits + adversarial skeptic verification on the top findings). Full report with file-level evidence: [docs/evidence/2026-09-11-desktop-product-adversarial-review.md](docs/evidence/2026-09-11-desktop-product-adversarial-review.md). Read it in full before acting — this is the short version.

**Verdict, confirmed by independent re-verification against the live repo (not just one agent's read):** the operator's confusion is correct. The two desktop apps are not two products — they're the same Electron shell loading the identical `renderer/` code, and once the engine starts, the identical Next.js web app. The only real difference is `edition.json`, which sets an env var the engine reads to hide 7 sidebar pages for Product. That filter is stale: `parity`, `search`, `system`, and `desktop` all call `ADMIN_ONLY` backend routes per `src/pravrudhi/api/roles.py` but were never added to `palette.ts`'s `STUDIO_ONLY_PAGES`/`PALETTE_PAGES`, so they render for a product user and only 404 when they try to fetch data. That's the direct, confirmed cause of "why do I get almost the same interface."

**Also confirmed:** the product edition's sign-in/workspace/artifact feature (`app/desktop/lib/product.js`) is fully implemented but never wired through `preload.js`/`main.js` — every user, every time, hits "Your workspace is not connected in this build yet." Dead feature, not a bug in use.

**Two findings my review agents raised were adversarially refuted, so don't act on them as stated:** the "/models page shows a browser-verification error" claim was a stale 2026-09-08 test artifact against a framework mismatch, not a live defect; the "first-run with no engine has zero guidance" claim is overstated — there is a permanent install-instructions link and a locate-engine button, just an unpolished flow.

**Unverified leads worth triaging yourself** (in the doc, not skeptic-checked): a second hosted web app (`vercel.json`, `NEXT_PUBLIC_DEMO=1`) sits undeployed-by-CI alongside the actively-maintained GitHub Pages recording, with nothing in the repo saying which is canonical; the Electron shell never tells the Next.js frontend it's running inside Electron, so a product user can click the in-app `/desktop` nav link and get told to install the app they're already running; ADR-0031's committed Tauri-vs-Electron spike was never recorded as attempted or aborted; edition detection silently defaults to Product on a malformed `edition.json` with no warning; the packaged smoke test never exercises the product IPC bridge, so the dead workspace feature above would pass smoke today.

**Short-term fixes I'd prioritize** (full list in the doc): make `STUDIO_ONLY_PAGES` derived from `roles.py`'s `ADMIN_ONLY` set with a test that fails on drift, instead of a hand-maintained list that goes stale every time a new operator page ships; gate at the page component level too, not just the sidebar (direct URL nav defeats it entirely); wire or delete the product IPC bridge — shipping it broken is worse than not shipping it; pick one canonical hosted URL and either finish Vercel's CI wiring or delete the dead config.

**Long-term, the actual architectural fix:** stop treating Product as "Studio minus some pages" (opt-out, leaks by default) and invert it to an explicit allowlist of what a product install renders at all (opt-in). That's the structural reason this bug class keeps recurring every time a new internal page ships.

**What I need from you:** check this against your own backlog/RSI state first — the same instruction as last time, don't redo what's already tracked. **Cloudflare Tunnel + Worker + KV pattern**, from `~/projects/game-llm/scripts/gateway/README.md` (a sibling project, same operator): a Cloudflare Worker at a stable domain (`kinetic.kinetic-ai.workers.dev`) is the permanent public front door. This is why every page shows "No engine reachable" even though the engine itself is healthy (curl to `/api/health` returns 200 fine). What's actually happening:

- Anonymous requests (no `Authorization` header) don't need a CORS preflight and succeed — that's why curl and a plain unauthenticated `fetch()` both work.
- Once signed in, the frontend attaches `Authorization: Bearer <supabase jwt>` to its API calls, which forces a real CORS preflight (`OPTIONS`) — and the engine rejects it outright.
- I reproduced this directly: `OPTIONS /api/health` with `Access-Control-Request-Headers: authorization,content-type` gets HTTP 400, body **"Disallowed CORS headers"**. The response's own `access-control-allow-headers` list is: `Accept, Accept-Language, Content-Language, Content-Type, x-pravrudhi-operator, x-pravrudhi-token` — no `Authorization`.

roster.note: Costs nothing and, on the evidence so far, does little: it produced no change at all on two tasks a hosted agent completed in minutes. Serving text and driving an agentic tool-calling loop are different capabilities. Restored to the mechanical tier only, and declared behind sonnet, so it is reached solely when the paid route is cooling. Last resort, not a peer.

The same Lite Plan, its cheap high-throughput model. Added 2026-09-08 after the plan's one-week quota was exhausted inside a day. The cause was not one expensive call: qwen3.8-max, the vendor's FLAGSHIP, was the declared first choice at both mechanical and standard, driving agent loops whose steps cost about 20,000 tokens each (one measured step of a trivial task: 20,419 total, 19,584 read from cache), dispatched hourly. Mechanical work is what a fast cheap model is for. The two share one quota, so this buys no capacity; it lowers the burn rate for the work that never needed the flagship, which is most of it. Admitted at mechanical only -- the same tier the plan's other model earned on one verified tool call -- because a cheaper model is not thereby a better one.

Alibaba's Lite Plan flagship, on a plan-exclusive endpoint with its own key file and a credit budget rather than a free-tier token cap. Verified live on 2026-09-07: given a file and a read tool it called the tool and returned the right answer, exit 0 in 8.6s. Admitted at the two tiers the free-tier loop was admitted at, on the same evidence and the same reasoning -- one verified tool call says the loop runs, not that it does design or critical work well. It is declared ahead of the free-tier loop because it is cheaper and the vendor's stronger model, and it rises further only on its measured record here.

A hosted free-tier model with no CLI: it cannot drive a tool-calling loop, only answer once with a JSON payload of whole-file contents. It is the SENTINEL. Permitted at every tier but declared last everywhere above mechanical, so the router reaches it only when every paid route at that tier is cooling down from a usage limit. A single-shot writer is a poor substitute for an agent loop and a far better one than a stopped loop, which is what the operator asked for on 2026-09-06: the system must run unattended when the paid accounts are spent. It stays because the loop above it is a different route and can also be spent.

Out of the tiers since 2026-09-08: the free tier's coding quota is spent. Asked to do work it answers "The free quota has been exhausted", observed through the agent rather than assumed, so it is a route the swarm can no longer choose. The subscribed Lite Plan (qwen-lite-max) is the Alibaba seat that works and is first at both tiers it serves. Kept here rather than deleted because the quota resets and the record of what it did is worth keeping. Qwen driving a real tool loop through OpenCode against DashScope Singapore. Verified live on 2026-09-07: given a file and a read tool it called the tool and returned the right answer, exit 0 in 8.1s at zero cost. An earlier attempt from inside a sandboxed agent failed at OpenCode's own log file before reaching DashScope, which is a property of nesting one agent inside another's sandbox and not of this route; agents/ALIBABA_LOOP.md keeps that transcript. Admitted at mechanical and standard because one verified tool call is evidence the loop runs, not evidence it does design or critical work well. It rises through the same measured outcomes as every other route, or it does not rise.

Cheapest route that can drive an agent loop, and demoted to no tier on the operator's instruction of 2026-09-06 ("don't go to too basic models"): it produced nothing on the tool-registry task that sonnet's sibling tasks completed. Kept in the table so the router can be told to try it again deliberately.
Measured 0.4951 on the same trivial prompt that cost sonnet 0.2117.

The strongest available and the only model this account's codex will accept. Twenty sessions in one day consumed seven million input tokens while it was the silent default for three of the four tiers. It is no longer permitted below the design tier.
